items.title: I made dinner. It made the post.
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I recorded a 47-second clip asking for a reel. Then I went and started dinner.

While the water was heating up, the thing cut the video, wrote the captions, checked it for anything it shouldn't put out, and posted it to Instagram.

It went live at 4:44. I was in the kitchen. Nobody was in the room.

Here's the part I keep chewing on: I didn't get faster. I got removed. The bottleneck was never the editing or the uploading — it was me, deciding to sit down and do it.

Most of what I call being busy is just me being the only one who can do the thing.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: The devil's weapon is ambivalence
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The devil doesn't need to ruin your life. He just needs you to wait.

Napoleon Hill wrote about this in Outwitting the Devil — he figured 98% of people are drifters. Not bad people. Just people who never quite decided, and handed the choice over to circumstances instead.

Then the hesitating hardens. He called it hypnotic rhythm: indecision stops being a moment and becomes the default setting.

Here's the part that got me. You're not delaying a choice. You're conditioning yourself to be paralyzed.

So whatever you've been sitting on — it is costing you more to not decide than it would cost you to decide wrong and move.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Money is not the root of all evil
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

"Money is the root of all evil." A friend said it to me today, and I want to squash it — because I think that sentence quietly stops a lot of good people from ever going after what they want.

Money is a modality. It's a tool. It's how we measure value moving through the world.

It amplifies whatever you're already holding. So yes — it will magnify evil that was already in there. That's not the same as causing it.

Here's the question worth sitting with: did evil exist before money did?

If it did, then money can't be the root of it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: The wrong decision beats indecision
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The wrong decision beats indecision. Not as a motivational line — as a metabolic one.

Dr. Martin Picard studies mitochondria at Columbia. The short version: everything costs energy, including the things you don't do. Sitting in ambivalence isn't free. It's expensive.

One honest caveat, and I say it in the video too — I'm recalling the number from memory and I could be off. Take the figure as my recollection, not a citation. The direction is the part I'd stake something on.

So decide. You can correct a wrong turn. You can't correct a car that never left the driveway.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.caption:

Nothing clever about it. It just means the six-month tighten-up actually happens, because the excuse is gone.

items.title: Give the value away
items.caption:

I see folks out on the corners holding signs. And I see clients, and I see patients, doing a version of the same thing.

Here's what I think they have in common, and I'm including myself in this. Every single person is holding something valuable. And we keep it tight. We keep it buried where nobody can get at it.

That's the mistake. Not that you don't have anything worth giving — that you're sitting on it.

So give it away. Give, give, give. That's the part I'm still working on.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: God-sized goals — the not-knowing is the point
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

If you already know how to reach it, it isn't a goal. It's a task.

I heard Dan Martell describe carrying goals so big he has no idea how he'd pull them off — and that the size is the whole point. Big enough that his ceiling ends up being somebody else's floor.

The part that got me wasn't the ambition. It was what comes after: you have to hand it over. Not the plan — you don't have a plan. The not-knowing.

I've spent years treating "I don't know how" as a reason to shrink the goal back down to something I could picture. He's saying that's backwards. Not knowing how is the evidence you finally picked a real one.

So pick the one you can't figure out yet. Then stop trying to figure it out before you start.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Just-in-case people vs just-in-time people
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

There are just-in-case people and there are just-in-time people.

Just-in-case waits until he's sure. One more book, one more course, one more year of getting ready — waiting to become the guy who'd be qualified to start.

Just-in-time moves, and works it out on the way down.

I was just-in-case for a long time and I called it being responsible. It wasn't. It was fear with a respectable job title.

Here's the part nobody mentions: the certainty you're waiting on doesn't show up before the action. It shows up because of it.

Wrong action, messy action, or a slam dunk — matters far less than moving. You can steer something that's rolling. You can't steer something parked.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

Open your calendar before noon and delete one recurring thing. Just one. That's addition by subtraction.

items.title: The bird and the twig (NF)
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I was patching walls in my son's room, listening to his music — an artist called NF — and one idea wouldn't let go.

I'll brutalize the quote, and I say so in the video too. It goes something like this: do you know why a bird perches on a twig? Is it because it trusts the twig to hold its weight? Or because it trusts its own ability to fly away?

Most of us spend our lives testing twigs. Checking if the job is safe, if the market is safe, if the timing is safe.

The bird doesn't audit the twig. It knows what its wings can do.

Think about that.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Willpower is finite — the Swiss cheese model
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The gift bags called me out. There WAS a system — and it's broken, because it ran on willpower.

A system that relies on willpower is bound to break. Willpower is finite. One bad day, one bad week, and the energy that was holding the whole thing together is gone.

So you don't build one perfect layer. You build layers, plural. In medicine it's called the Swiss cheese model: every layer has holes, but you stack them so the holes don't line up. More layers, fewer things get through — and when something breaks, it's an easy fix instead of a collapse.

Stop blaming your discipline. Start stacking layers.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Every system dies at 3 months
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Willpower is finite — so a system that runs on willpower alone will break.

When I read Traction and Rocket Fuel, the whole EOS world said the same thing out loud: expect the willpower to fall short at about three months. That's not failure, that's just how humans run. I've watched the same pattern in my PT practice.

The fix isn't a better system. It's a standing appointment with the system: a quarterly meeting to re-inspire it, spot what's about to break, and fix it while it's still cheap to fix.

Put the check-up on the calendar before you need it.

So now they get the list instead. Backpack? Glove? Bat? Shoes - because you don't want sand in there and you want to run fast.

items.title: The Alchemist - beginner's luck isn't luck
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Storytime. The Alchemist, page 54.

The merchant tells the boy business is good - soon you'll be able to go back to your sheep. Why ask more out of life? And the boy answers before he means to: because we have to respond to omens.

Then he regrets saying it, because the merchant never met the king.

Coelho calls it the principle of favorability. Beginner's luck. Life tilts toward you at the start because it wants you to go after your personal legend.

Here's my read on it. Even when it doesn't feel like a lesson, it's refinement. It's preparing you for the next one - the next opportunity in your life's true purpose.

And the part I keep coming back to: the more you succeed, the more the rest of the world succeeds.

So go get it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

Here's where I think it goes amiss: we feel like we need to play other roles. We don't. We just need to stop thinking we do.

Accept yourself, and you'll find yourself surrounded by people who accept you too. And watch what happens to the people who required you to be someone else.

Here's the funny thing: the only reason the idea that we're alone can hurt us is that it IS an idea.

We're all part of one big, beautiful ocean. One molecule colliding with another moves the next one. It's a wave. (You love water analogies. I love water analogies.)

So — you're not alone. And if hearing that stings a little, that twinge is a signal. There's a rumor in your mind worth dispelling. I want you to win, because the more free you feel, the more it ripples to the rest of us.

The only price is being at peace with letting go of the old ones.

Overhead work with one hand: a deep socket on a ratchet, right through the eye hole.

items.title: Two books, one door — infinite intelligence
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Two books, written sixty years apart, describing the same thing without ever agreeing to.

The Alchemist calls it the soul of the earth. Napoleon Hill calls it infinite intelligence. I'm about halfway through Outwitting the Devil right now and I keep landing on the same page twice.

I don't have this figured out. I'm telling you what I noticed, not what I concluded.

But when two people who never met describe the same door, I stop asking whether the door is real and start asking how you get through it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Move one centimeter today
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Everything I've learned that actually mattered is stuff we've all heard a million times and decided to turn a deaf ear to.

It's your habits. Your everyday habits. Doing the ordinary thing on purpose instead of by accident.

And here's the number that made it doable for me: a centimeter. Not a leap, not a transformation. Move one centimeter toward your purpose today.

The part I keep having to relearn — you can fulfil your purpose every single day. You don't need to wait until you hit a certain level, a certain income. Those make it easier to do at scale. They were never the permission slip.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: My purpose is to empower others — and the gap
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

As far as I know myself, my purpose is to empower other people.

And I fulfil it every day. Almost everyone in the medical world does, to an extent — it's built into the work.

So the gap isn't that I'm not doing it. The gap is that I don't believe I'm doing it at the level I'm capable of.

That's an uncomfortable thing to say out loud, because it isn't a complaint about circumstances. It's just true, and it's mine to fix.

I'm on that journey with intention now.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

Free tools — full list in my profile.

items.title: I made it far too easy to drift
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I was on this journey earlier in my life. And then I wasn't.

Not because of one decision. Because I built — the way most people build — an environment where drifting was just far too easy. Nothing dramatic. Easy is the whole danger.

And I'm sorry. To a lot of people, and to myself, for those years.

Because it looks to me like my impact could have been much greater, much sooner. And a lot of pain could have been avoided — at minimum in my life, and in the lives of the people standing closest to me.

I'm not telling you this for sympathy. I'm telling you because the drift is quiet while it's happening, and somebody has to say that out loud.

Lead with intention. Keep your purpose in mind. You will not be subject to drifting.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

Free tools — full list in my profile.

items.title: The third hand — you don't need help, you need a setup
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I'm in the garage building racks for two canoes and I leave in the morning. Nobody's holding the other end of anything.

So every trick in here is really the same trick: quit trying to be a second person, and build something that holds it for you. A stop block holds the measurement so you never measure twice. A clamp gives you a lip you can trust. Screws set first mean nothing has to be lined up and held at the same time.

Then the one I keep forgetting — my own hands. Years of telling patients their body is the best instrument they own, and there I am reaching for a tape measure to find a center my fingertips already know.

It's wood. It's near perfect. It goes on the truck in the morning.

One dad hack every day. Follow so you stop losing the next one.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Less moving parts equals more fingers on your hand
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The scariest second on a miter saw isn't the cut. It's after it.

Lock the blade down so the cut is honest. Snug it up. Then cut slow — because once you're in, you're trapped in the wood, and the only good news is the saw is pushing the wood into the fence.

And the rule I don't break: the blade is completely stopped before I release. Not slowing. Stopped.

Less moving parts equals more fingers on your hand.

A hack a day. Follow and never miss one.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: A dull pencil costs you a sixteenth of an inch
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

You can measure perfectly and still be off, and it isn't the tape's fault.

A dull pencil costs you about a sixteenth of an inch. Sharper pencil, better line. A marking knife is better still.

And the one that changed my marks: put the pencil on the target first, then bring the square to the pencil. Most of us do it backwards — set the square, then chase it with the lead.

Center is just corner to corner, twice. Draw the line. There's center.

The hack I wish I'd had. Free, every day — follow.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Just start — the next best path becomes obvious
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

An engineer's job is to make it work, not to make it perfect.

Then the board split. On camera, hours before I load the truck. I drilled too shallow, too close to the surface, and it let go.

Here's the part I'd have missed if I'd planned longer: I only learned the right hole depth by splitting one. If you don't know what you're doing, just start and get at it — the next best path becomes pretty obvious. You get a lot farther sooner than if you spent a ton of time thinking about it.

You'll forget this by Thursday. Follow instead.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: It worked — the roof rack came home
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Five nights in the Boundary Waters. The rack I built alone in the garage the morning before we left — stop blocks, clamps, screws set first — carried two canoes up and back without a shrug.

That's the whole reason to build the setup instead of white-knuckling the load: you stop having to hold it. It holds while you're gone.

Sorry to anyone waiting on a free canoe on the side of the highway. Not this trip.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Ratchet straps: fold, fold, figure eight
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Ratchet strap spaghetti is a choice. Fold the strap in half, in half again 'til it's a foot or two long, tie a loose figure eight, toss it in the bag. The most it ever tangles is one hook.

Thirty seconds of putting away buys back the minutes you'd spend swearing at a knot with the canoe half loaded.

The setup does the remembering so you don't have to.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Keep tension before the first crank
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Fair warning: I'm an idiot — it took me almost 40 years to learn you can keep tension on a ratchet strap before your first crank. Feed the tail through, wrap it around, pull the slack. Now the strap holds itself while you crank.

One more time the answer wasn't try harder, hold tighter, be two people. It was set it up so it can't go slack.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: No phone for 4 days. It posted anyway.
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I was in a canoe with no phone, no internet, no laptop for four days. This page posted three times a day the whole time.

Not magic — snippets like this one, recorded when I have ten free minutes, dropped in a folder. The system I built cuts them, captions them, posts them, and doesn't need me to be home.

Same lesson as the roof rack: build the thing once, and it holds while you're gone.

Free tools — full list in my profile.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Less moving parts, more fingers
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Same morning as the canoe racks. A bunch of repeat cuts, and the two rules that kept all ten fingers on my hands: lock the blade down, and cut slow — because after the cut you're trapped in the wood, and the saw only leaves politely if nothing else is moving.

Less moving parts equals more fingers on your hand. That's the whole safety course.

More accurate, less tedious too. At least I hope so.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: The no-split screw trick: reverse first
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Screws splitting your boards? Dent it to start, back the screw out in reverse for a second, then drive it home. I think the physics is it warms up the hole — honestly I'm not sure, and you can hear the hedge on tape.

What I am sure of: no splits.

Works every time, about 50% of the time.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: How it started — 30 inches too narrow
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

This is Saturday's rack, back before it worked. Roof bars 50 inches wide, two canoes that needed 80. A bracket, a 2x4, 15 more inches a side, the day before we left.

You already know the ending — it came home. This is what the middle of building something looks like: one secured, three teed up, no guarantee.

To be continued.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: They called me the resident knot guy. I know two.
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I came back from the canoe trip with a new title: resident knot guy of the trip. I know two knots.

That's the whole thing. It was never about knowing forty knots. If you can make a loop, you can secure just about anything -- feed the loop, let it catch on its own knot, and the harder it pulls the tighter it holds. Easy to set, easy to undo.

Most problems I hit out there weren't strength problems. They were setup problems.

One dad hack a day. Follow so you stop losing the next one.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: In the rabbit hole, around the tree trunk, back
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The bowline, the way it was taught to me: the rabbit comes out of the hole, around the tree trunk, and back down the hole. Pull it tight and you get a little pretzel shape. That shape is how you know you got it right.

What you end up with is a loop that holds its size under load instead of cinching down on whatever is inside it.

I'm not a knot guy. I just know that loops are very helpful.

There's one of these every day. Follow so you've got the knot before the day you need it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Canoe storage for ten bucks
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

You pick up a canoe, dream about all the adventures you'll have, and then store it about twelve months of the year. Maybe take it out for a week. Me too.

So it hangs under the deck now. A carabiner, some rope, an eye hole -- less than ten bucks. Off the ground, protected from the sun, and it isn't leaning against the house anymore.

The trip is the fun part. The setup is what makes the next trip easy to say yes to.

I post the one I wish somebody had told me. Every day. Free.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: The absence was the signal
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

A kid decides what a lesson means, and nobody ever checks the answer.

The father thinks he is teaching self-reliance. The son is learning he isn't important. Neither of them says it out loud, so the silence gets filed as normal, and twenty years later the relationship is just... absent.

That absence WAS the signal. It always is.

Heed the omens, fathers. If I'm being honest, that's my biggest fear -- a disconnected relationship with my own kids.

One a day. Follow or lose it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Your relationship with failure
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Here's the question nobody asks out loud: what is your relationship with failure?

Because you are not actually scared of the risk. You are scared of what failing would mean about you.

Change the label on the task -- this is practice data, or this is a test -- and the whole thing gets cheaper. A healthy relationship with failure means you take the swing, because you trust yourself to grow from it and show up better prepared next time.

I post the one I wish somebody had told me. Every day. Free.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Same fight, two scoreboards
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Been chewing on a movie where a father and a son spend the whole story fighting, and the fight is not the wound.

The wound is that they were never keeping the same score. He thought he was teaching. The kid thought he did not matter. Same twenty years, two different scoreboards.

Then they find the same scoreboard in about ninety seconds at a dinner table. Twenty years of holding a narrative, undone in ninety seconds -- and nobody wanted to speak up first.

One dad hack a day. Follow so you stop losing the next one.

items.title: The word that stopped my drift

I'm reading the one about the monk who sold his Ferrari, and the phrase that keeps landing on me is definiteness of purpose.

Don't drift. Be conscious in your movements. Be conscious in your actions.

And I have to say it out loud: I'm drifting. Some people call it shiny object syndrome.

Here's what caught me. My kids live in definiteness of purpose. Their purpose might only be the next four hours. But they live and die for it — which is why if it ever comes down to a battle of wills between a kid and a grown adult, the kid wins.

items.title: The power isn't where you think
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I based a lot of my life in facts and measures. Eight years and a doctorate, learning facts. So I still struggle day to day with believing in a higher power.

But here's where I've landed. If God is the personification of all that is good, and you believe He'll take care of you no matter what — that everything put in your path is meant for you, for improving yourself, for fulfilling your potential, for staying on purpose — then that is power.

The power isn't necessarily in God. It's in the faith that God's got your back. And that gives you the power to do what you need to do to accomplish the thing.

I flip-flop on this still today. Do I truly believe in a higher power — or am I using that as an excuse to not believe in myself?

Even if I'm using the idea of God as a filter, or a mirror to reflect back my own power and ability, and to have faith in myself — does it really matter? The end result should be the same, right?

I think it's harder to hold that line, though, when it's just you and yourself.

There's one of these every day. You're either getting them or you're not.

items.title: It's already built

items.title: He only needs to delay you

The devil doesn't need to defeat you. He only needs to delay you.

I'm in the chapter of Outwitting the Devil where Hill interviews him, and it is rough reading. Every page it's yep, guilty of that. Yep, guilty of that.

items.title: Volume beats polish
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I was sitting with two people who wanted to see the thing actually work, so I gave them the only honest demo there is: I recorded a video about recording a video, dropped it in a folder, and walked away from it.

No script. No second take. My eyes are on the screen instead of the lens for half of it.

Here is what I have stopped apologizing for. The post that goes up beats the post that is still being polished. Volume and distribution come first. Quality shows up on the reps - it does not show up on the first one, and waiting for it is just a nicer word for not posting.

Most people do not have a quality problem. They have a never-hit-publish problem.

items.title: The tool that outwits every turn
items.caption:

The reframe.

items.title: The tool or the carpenter?
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

A question I couldn't put down today.

Does the tool the carpenter uses define the quality of the job? Or is it the skill of the carpenter?

The tool helps. A good one lets an unskilled hand step things up a little.

But all that to say: you don't need fancy tools. You have everything you need already. You just need the skill -- and you need to refine and sharpen your mind.

No new gear required. One of these a day. Follow and use them.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Your most important tool

What's the most important tool in your arsenal?

It's your mind. And you've got to keep it sharp.

So on that note -- I put a shelf of free tools on the site for exactly that. Not theory. The ones I'm actually using, the ones I found useful on my own journey.

items.title: The book they buried for two generations
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Outwitting the Devil, by Napoleon Hill.

The part I can't put down isn't the book. It's the story behind the story.

For two generations nobody was allowed to read it. The people in control of Hill's estate refused to let it be published -- because of what it contained, and the blowback they thought would come.

Written roughly the late 1930s. Not published until 2011.

If that's not a statement of how powerful words are, I don't know what is. Not necessarily these words -- but I believe them to be pretty powerful.

So be mindful of the words you surround yourself with.

I post the one I wish somebody had told me. Every day. Free.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Fear and faith start the same
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

A question I couldn't put down today.

Is it by coincidence that fear and faith sit on opposite sides of the spectrum -- but begin with the same letter?

That's the whole thought. No tidy answer attached.

Think about it, Dad.

You'll forget this by Thursday. Follow and you won't have to remember it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Make the mistake look on purpose
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I put a nick in the wood. Right on the face, right where anyone would look.

The old move is to start over. Cut new stock, lose the afternoon, call it doing it right.

Instead I ran a router around the whole edge. Every side gets the same profile now -- and that nick is pretty much gone. Not hidden. Absorbed.

That's the part nobody teaches you. Sometimes you don't fix the mistake. You change the standard until the mistake belongs.

One dad hack a day. Follow so you stop losing the next one.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Nobody sees the back
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

That's the back of the frame. I didn't clean it up. There was no need -- nobody sees the back.

Some imperfection. Not terrible.

The front gets the sanding, the routing, the second look. The back gets to be what it is. That isn't laziness, it's knowing which surface is load-bearing.

Then you hold it up and it goes together like it was made to fit.

One hack a day. Follow, and keep the one you need.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: A 1938 book and modern brain science
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Napoleon Hill wrote Outwitting the Devil in 1938.

Read it next to the ten principles of neuroplasticity -- the rules for how a brain actually rewires -- and they run almost hand in hand. Same mechanics, decades before anyone could image a brain to check them.

I'm not going to tell you what that means. Make your own comparison and think for yourself.

One a day. Free. Follow, keep up.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: You don't get to choose your purpose
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I don't think we get to choose our purpose.

We get to choose whether or not to discover it. We get to choose whether or not to carry it out. That part is actually ours.

And the souls on this earth who choose not to pursue it -- even a centimeter a day -- are left feeling pain, unfulfillment.

It does start with some awareness though. If there's something inside your heart, inside your soul, that says there's something missing: I think that's purpose calling.

An idea a day. Follow, hear it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Quit calling it good or bad
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I'm growing to hate "good" and "bad." Not the words - the habit.

Because both of them are judgments, and honestly? I am not well equipped to pass judgment. Neither is anybody I've met. We call a thing bad on Tuesday and thank God for it by Christmas.

So I swapped the question.

Instead of "was that good or bad," I ask: is this in alignment with what I want to get done in this life?

That question has an answer. The other one just has an argument.

And when the answer is no, I don't have to hate it. I just don't have to carry it either.

Try it on the thing that's been sitting on your chest all week. Not good, not bad. Aligned, or not.

There's one of these every day. You're either getting them or you're not.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Pain is a signal
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Something happened this year that hurt, and I caught myself wanting to file it under "bad" and walk away.

Here's where I landed instead: that pain is a signal.

Not a verdict. Not a punishment. A signal - the same way a smoke alarm isn't the fire.

It's telling me something is out of alignment. And the move isn't to sit in it, and it isn't to numb it. The move is action. Focused action, in one specific direction, like a laser.

Scattered action is just anxiety with a to-do list.

So when it hurts this week, ask the alarm what it's pointing at. Then go do that one thing.

I post the one I wish somebody had told me. Every day. Free.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Why we invent monsters
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I've been deep in Outwitting the Devil, and I want to be honest about something: I'm not sure I believe there is an actual devil.

But here's what I keep coming back to. Human minds are terrible at fighting a fog. We are very good at fighting a face.

So we build one. We take the thing that is vague and heavy and undefeatable, and we give it horns - not because we're simple, but because a monster is something you can actually beat.

You can't conquer "a bad season." You can conquer a villain.

That's not superstition. That's a man handing himself something to win against, which is the only way anybody ever gets to be their own hero.

Name yours this week. It gets smaller the second it has a shape.

One dad hack a day. Follow so you stop losing the next one.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: The joke cost me my point
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I'm a poet and I didn't even know it.

That's the whole joke. And it cost me the actual point I was about to make, which I have still not recovered.

Here's the thing though. That book sat unpublished for 73 years - finished in 1938, didn't reach a bookstore until 2011. Seventy-three years of patience for one idea.

And I couldn't hold my own thought for nine seconds because a rhyme showed up.

I'm not going to pretend that's a lesson. Sometimes you just lose the plot to a dad joke and laugh at yourself in the car.

If you're the kind of dad who does this too, you're in the right place.

One of these every day. Follow so you stop losing them.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Don't tell them the lesson
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I caught myself doing the thing you did - handing over a lesson and assuming the meaning came with it. It doesn't. The lesson lands; the meaning gets invented.

So I'm trying something. I say the thing, and then I shut up and ask.

"How'd that feel?"
"What'd it mean to you?"
"What'd you learn?"

We don't get to decide the meaning for our kids. We only get to decide whether we're still in the room when they pick one.

One dad hack a day. Follow so you stop losing the next one.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Know a problem property?
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Somebody reading this knows a house that has turned into a weight. A rental that stopped being worth it. A place somebody inherited and cannot get to.

If it sits in Washington or Dakota County, Minnesota, I would like to hear about it. I have a network of people looking specifically in those areas, and often there is enough room in a deal that everybody walks away better than they came in.

I am not asking anybody to sell me anything. I am asking for a conversation.

Know one? Send me a DM.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Their brain fills in the blank
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Here is the part of this nobody warned me about. A lesson handed over without a reason does not land as a lesson. It lands as a blank.

And a kid's nervous system does not leave blanks empty. Out of pure self-protection it fills them, and it reaches for the scariest, most painful thing it can find.

So the silence where the why should have been is not neutral. It is an invitation.

Give them the intention, not just the instruction.

One of these a day. Follow, take it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Shade you'll never sit in
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Blessed are those who plant trees under whose shade they will never sit.

I keep coming back to that one. The test of whether you are actually building something is not whether it works. It is whether it still works after you are gone from it.

Not for you. For the future.

One dad hack a day. Follow, get it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Looking for a church
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Buildings get built to hold people. Then one day the doors stay shut, and everybody drives past it like it was always empty.

I'm a real estate investor, and that's the kind of building I'm hunting: a church in Dakota County or Washington County, Minnesota. Not to strip it. To put a purpose back in something that already had one.

If you know of one sitting empty - or somebody sitting on one and stuck - that's the whole buy box. A church. Dakota or Washington County, MN.

Message me and we'll go from there.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: How drifting actually starts
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Nobody wakes up and decides to waste a decade. That's not how it goes.

It goes like this: you do a thing with a little less purpose behind it than you had yesterday. Then a little less intention. There are degrees of it, and every single degree feels reasonable at the time.

That's drifting. It never announces itself. It just quietly takes the wheel.

The fix isn't dramatic. It's vigilance and diligence on the boring days, when nobody is watching and nothing is on fire. It's hard. It's also the only thing that works.

One of these every day. Follow or you miss tomorrow's.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.
